title: Recent stressful life events and youth self‐regulation: Environmental risk or shared genetic liability?
abstract: Abstract Adolescence is a period of heightened exposure to stressful life events (SLEs) and rapid maturation of self‐regulation, yet the etiology of this association remains unclear. Using a longitudinal twin design, this study examined genetic and shared environmental contributions to recent SLEs at age 13 and four self‐regulation domains at age 14 (activation control, attentional focusing, inhibitory control, impulsivity). Univariate models revealed etiologic heterogeneity: recent SLEs fit a shared and nonshared environmental (CE) model, activation control, attentional focusing, and impulsivity fit additive genetic and nonshared environmental (AE) models, and inhibitory control fit comparable AE and CE models. Bivariate models consistently indicated additive genetic overlap between recent SLEs and all four self‐regulation domains. Findings highlight the multidimensional etiology of adolescent self‐regulation and suggest that SLEs–self‐regulation associations partly reflect gene–environment correlation processes. Importantly, genetic overlap does not imply that stressful experiences themselves are genetically determined, but rather may reflect genetically influenced person–environment transactions involved in adolescents' exposure to, appraisal of, or responses to stressful experiences.
